why: He described the tube linking the middle ear to the throat.
mean: Of the tube joining the middle ear to the back of the throat
story: An Italian anatomist working before the printing of good anatomical plates described the narrow tube that lets the middle ear equalise pressure. It is why your ears pop in a lift, and it has carried his name for four centuries.

why: He described the tubes running from ovary to womb.
mean: Of the pair of tubes carrying eggs from ovary to womb
story: An Italian anatomist who died at thirty-nine described the delicate tubes running from ovary to womb, comparing their flared ends to trumpets. He got the function wrong but the anatomy right, and the tubes still bear his name.

why: He described the microscopic canals running through compact bone.
mean: Of the tiny canals carrying blood vessels through compact bone
story: An English physician put thin slices of bone under an early microscope and found it was not solid at all but drilled through with a network of tiny tunnels carrying blood vessels. Bone turned out to be plumbing, and the canals took his name.

why: He described the onion-layered pressure receptors in deep tissue.
mean: Of the layered receptors deep in skin that sense pressure and vibration
story: An Italian anatomist found onion-layered capsules buried deep in the skin and joints that fire when pressed or vibrated. He also saw the cholera bacterium thirty years before Koch, and got credit for neither in his lifetime.

why: He described the fluid-filled follicle that releases an egg.
mean: Of the fluid-filled ovarian follicle that releases a mature egg
story: A Dutch physician described the fluid-filled blisters on the ovary and argued they held the egg. He was nearly right: they hold the follicle that releases it. He died at thirty-two, embittered by a priority quarrel with a colleague.

why: He gave his name to structures in the kidney, spleen and insect gut.
mean: Of several microscopic structures in kidney, spleen or insect excretory system
story: An Italian microscopist was the first to see capillaries, red blood cells and the filtering knots of the kidney. So much of the invisible body was his discovery that his name now attaches to structures in three separate organ systems.

why: He described the oil glands along the rim of the eyelid.
mean: Of the oil glands lining the rim of the eyelid
story: A German physician described rows of tiny oil glands along the eyelid margin. Their oil stops tears evaporating too fast; when they clog, eyes feel gritty and dry. Modern eye clinics still name the condition after him.

why: He described the small extra bones found in skull sutures.
mean: Of the small extra bones sometimes found within skull sutures
story: A Danish physician described the small irregular islands of bone that sometimes form inside the wavy joints of the skull. They are harmless in most people but crowd in on certain bone diseases, which is why radiologists still count them.

why: He described the deep cleft dividing the temporal lobe from the rest of the brain.
mean: Of the deep fissure separating the temporal lobe of the brain
story: A Dutch physician traced the deep cleft that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. It is the most obvious landmark on the side of the human brain, and the artery running along it carries his name too.

why: He described the central furrow dividing motor from sensory cortex.
mean: Of the central furrow of the brain dividing motor from sensory cortex
story: An Italian anatomist mapped the deep furrow running down the top of the brain. In front of it lies the strip that commands movement; behind it, the strip that receives touch. A whole class of childhood epilepsy is named from that furrow.

why: He gave his name to fibres in the heart and to large neurons in the cerebellum.
mean: Of conducting fibres in the heart or large branching neurons in the cerebellum
story: A Czech physiologist who founded the world's first independent physiology department described both the fibres that carry the heart's electrical signal and the huge fan-shaped neurons of the cerebellum. Two entirely different cells carry the same name.

why: He described the cells that wrap nerve fibres in insulating sheaths.
mean: Of the cells that wrap peripheral nerve fibres in an insulating sheath
story: A German physiologist proposed that all animal tissue is built from cells, then found the ones that spiral around nerve fibres like insulation on wire. Without them a nerve signal would crawl instead of race.

who: an Italian physician and Nobel laureate (1843-1926)
why: His silver staining method revealed a stack of membranes inside the cell.
mean: Of the stack of membranes that packages proteins inside a cell
story: An Italian physician invented a silver stain that made single nerve cells stand out black against pale tissue. It won him a Nobel Prize shared with a rival he publicly disagreed with, and it revealed the cell's packaging depot, now named for him.

why: He described the scavenging cells lining the liver's blood channels.
mean: Of the scavenging immune cells lining the liver's blood channels
story: A Baltic German anatomist described star-shaped cells stationed in the liver's blood channels. They swallow bacteria and worn-out red cells as blood filters past, making the liver a checkpoint as well as a chemical works.

why: He described the nurse cells that support developing sperm.
mean: Of the nurse cells that support developing sperm cells
story: An Italian physiologist, still a student when he made the discovery, described tall cells in the testis that cradle developing sperm and feed them through their whole maturation. They are among the few true nurse cells in the body.

why: He described the testosterone-producing cells of the testis.
mean: Of the cells in the testis that produce testosterone
story: A German zoologist described clusters of cells sitting between the sperm-making tubes rather than inside them. Their job turned out to be chemical, not reproductive: they make the hormone that drives male development.

why: He described the touch receptor cells at the base of the epidermis.
mean: Of the touch-receptor cells at the base of the outer skin layer
story: A German anatomist described cells sitting at the base of the outer skin layer that report steady pressure and fine texture. They are why you can feel the difference between paper and silk with a fingertip.

why: He described the light-touch corpuscles just under the skin surface.
mean: Of the light-touch receptors just below the skin surface
story: A German anatomist described egg-shaped bundles of nerve endings packed just under hairless skin. They fire on the lightest brush and go quiet if the touch holds still, which is why you stop noticing your own clothes.

why: He described the stretch-sensing endings in skin and joint capsules.
mean: Of the receptors that sense sustained stretch in skin and joints
story: An Italian anatomist described spindle-shaped nerve endings that report sustained stretch rather than momentary touch. They tell your brain where your fingers are without your having to look, which is how you can type in the dark.

why: He described the capsule that collects filtrate in the kidney.
mean: Of the cup-shaped capsule that collects filtered fluid in the kidney
story: An English surgeon showed that the kidney works by filtering blood through a knot of capillaries into a cup, rather than by secreting urine directly. The cup is named after him and the filtering knot after Malpighi.

why: He described the hairpin loop in the kidney tubule that concentrates urine.
mean: Of the hairpin loop in the kidney tubule that concentrates urine
story: A German anatomist traced a hairpin bend in the kidney's tubules that dips down into the organ and back. The bend lets the kidney pull water back out of urine, which is why land animals can survive on so little of it.

why: He described the patches of lymph tissue in the wall of the small intestine.
mean: Of the patches of immune tissue in the wall of the small intestine
story: A Swiss anatomist described oval patches of immune tissue studding the lining of the small intestine. They sample everything passing through, which makes them the gut's border control and the first place typhoid attacks.

why: He described the alkaline-secreting glands of the duodenum.
mean: Of the glands in the duodenum that secrete protective alkaline mucus
story: A Swiss anatomist described glands in the first stretch of intestine that pump out alkaline mucus. Their job is defensive: they neutralise the flood of stomach acid before it can burn the gut wall downstream.

why: He described the nerve network in the gut wall that drives its muscle waves.
mean: Of the nerve network in the gut wall that drives its muscular waves
story: A German neuropathologist found a full nerve network woven between the muscle layers of the gut. It runs the waves that push food along without asking the brain, which is why the gut is sometimes called a second nervous system.

why: He located the brain region whose damage destroys comprehension of speech.
mean: Of the brain region essential for understanding language
story: A German neurologist found patients who spoke fluently in complete nonsense and could not understand a word said to them. The damage sat behind the ear, in a region that turns sound into meaning, and it carries his name.

why: He located the brain region whose damage destroys fluent speech.
mean: Of the brain region essential for producing fluent speech
story: A French physician examined a patient who understood everything but could say only one syllable. The autopsy showed a lesion in the left frontal lobe. It was the first hard evidence that a single mental function lives in one patch of brain.

why: He described the sensory organ of the inner ear that converts sound to nerve signals.
mean: Of the sensory organ of the inner ear that turns sound into nerve signals
story: An Italian anatomist dissected the spiral of the inner ear and found a ribbon of hair cells sitting on a membrane. Each responds to a different pitch, so the ear separates a chord into notes before the brain hears anything.

why: He described the accessory smell organ in the nasal cavity.
mean: Of the accessory smell organ in the nasal cavity of many animals
story: A Danish surgeon described a second smell organ tucked into the nasal cavity. In snakes and cats it reads chemical signals from other animals, which is why a snake flicks its tongue into the roof of its mouth.

why: He described the pair of lubricating glands at the vaginal opening.
mean: Of a pair of small lubricating glands near the vaginal opening
story: A Danish anatomist from a family of three generations of anatomists described a pair of pea-sized lubricating glands. His father named the lymphatic system's thoracic duct; the family put its surname on a remarkable amount of the body.

why: He described the pair of glands that secrete pre-ejaculatory fluid.
mean: Of a pair of small glands below the prostate
story: An English surgeon described a pair of pea-sized glands below the prostate. He also republished another anatomist's plates under his own name, causing one of the ugliest plagiarism rows in the history of anatomy.

why: He named the submandibular salivary duct and the jelly inside the umbilical cord.
mean: Of the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw
story: An English physician who stayed in London through the plague of 1665 while most doctors fled described the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw. The jelly that cushions the vessels inside an umbilical cord also carries his name.

why: He described the duct draining the parotid salivary gland.
mean: Of the duct draining the large salivary gland in front of the ear
story: A Danish anatomist found the duct draining the big salivary gland in front of the ear when he was twenty-two. He then left medicine, worked out how fossils form and how rock layers stack, and ended his life as a bishop.

why: He described the hormone-producing islands scattered through the pancreas.
mean: Of the clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas
story: A German medical student described strange islands of cells scattered through the pancreas and admitted he had no idea what they did. Forty years later they turned out to make insulin. He died of tuberculosis at forty-one.

who: an English physician and pioneer of neurology (1621-1675)
why: He described the ring of arteries supplying the base of the brain.
mean: Of the ring of arteries supplying blood to the base of the brain
story: An English physician traced a ring of arteries at the base of the brain that lets blood reach it from more than one direction. If one vessel blocks, the ring can reroute around it, which is why some strokes cause far less damage than expected.

why: He described the deep membranous layer of the abdominal wall.
mean: Of the deep membranous layer of the abdominal wall
story: An Italian anatomist described the deep membranous sheet in the abdominal wall that limits how far leaked fluid can spread. He was so disliked that after his death a colleague kept his severed head on display in the university museum.

why: He described the thickened band of tissue running to the groin.
mean: Of the thickened band of tissue running from hip to groin
story: A French surgeon described the thickened cord of tissue running from the hip bone to the pubic bone. Every hernia repair works around it, and the two kinds of groin hernia are distinguished by which side of it they emerge.

why: He described the ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the throat.
mean: Of the ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the entrance to the throat
story: A German anatomist described the ring of tonsils and lymph tissue circling the entrance to the throat, catching whatever is breathed or swallowed. He also coined the words neuron and chromosome, which outlasted the ring in fame.

why: He described the thin membrane dividing chambers of the inner ear.
mean: Of the thin membrane separating two fluid chambers of the inner ear
story: A Baltic German anatomist described a membrane just two cells thick separating two fluid chambers of the cochlear spiral. The fluids on either side carry different salts, and that difference is what powers hearing.

why: He described the membrane beneath the retina.
mean: Of the thin membrane lying beneath the retina
story: A German anatomist described the thin layered membrane between the retina and its blood supply. It thickens with age and cracks, and those cracks are where the blood vessels of macular degeneration break through.

why: He described the whorled bodies found in the thymus.
mean: Of the whorled cell bodies found in the thymus gland
story: An English microscopist described onion-like whorls of flattened cells buried in the thymus. He also used his microscope on London's drinking water, and his drawings of what lived in it helped force the city to build proper sewers.

why: His stain revealed granular bodies in the nerve cell body.
mean: Of the granular protein-making bodies stained inside a nerve cell
story: A German neuropathologist invented a dye that turned the protein factories inside nerve cell bodies deep blue. When a nerve is injured the granules scatter and fade, so the stain became a way of reading damage directly.

why: He described the giant motor neurons of the cerebral cortex.
mean: Of the giant motor neurons in the brain's movement cortex
story: A Ukrainian anatomist described the largest cells in the human cortex, giant neurons whose fibres run all the way down the spinal cord. Each one commands muscle directly, and a single cell can be a metre long.

why: He described the gaps in a nerve's insulating sheath where the signal jumps.
mean: Of the regular gaps in a nerve's insulating sheath
story: A French histologist noticed that the insulation around a nerve fibre is not continuous but broken by regular tiny gaps. The signal leaps from gap to gap instead of crawling along, which makes a nerve impulse fifty times faster.

why: He described the fibrous envelope around the kidney.
mean: Of the fibrous envelope surrounding the kidney
story: A Romanian surgeon described the fibrous envelope wrapping each kidney in its bed of fat. Surgeons still name the plane by him, because a tumour contained inside that envelope is a far better prospect than one that has broken out.

why: He described the fascial layer between rectum and prostate.
mean: Of the fascial layer lying between rectum and prostate
story: A French surgeon described a thin sheet of fascia separating the rectum from the prostate. Two centuries later it decides the outcome of prostate surgery: staying on the right side of that sheet is what spares the nerves.
